props.title: Dark Angel

sections.content: Dark Angel (1990), also released as "I Come in Peace" in some markets, exemplifies the height of late 80s/early 90s sci-fi action fusion. Starring Dolph Lundgren at his prime, it follows the formula established by Predator (1987) and The Hidden (1987) - tough cop versus alien threat. The film's distinctive angle comes from its drug-dealing alien antagonist who harvests human endorphins, creating a clever mashup of police thriller and extraterrestrial horror. Its neon-drenched Houston setting and synthesizer score by Jan Hammer (of Miami Vice fame) perfectly capture that specific moment in action cinema.

sections.content: The film sits within a specific subset of late 80s/early 90s sci-fi action that includes Split Second (1992) and Abraxas, Guardian of the Universe (1990). These films share a common DNA - musclebound heroes, otherworldly threats, urban settings, and practical effects that emphasize physical stunts over CGI. What sets Dark Angel apart is its commitment to proper sci-fi world-building, with alien weapons, distinct extraterrestrial designs, and a coherent if outlandish premise about intergalactic drug trafficking.

Director Craig R. Baxley, coming from a background in stunt coordination, brings the same kinetic energy he displayed in Action Jackson (1988). The film's action sequences emphasize practical explosions and hand-to-hand combat, following the template of other alien-on-Earth stories like Predator 2 (1990) and Peacemaker (1990), but with its own unique flourishes like the alien's lethal flying disc weapon. sections.content: While not achieving the cultural impact of contemporaries like RoboCop (1987) or Total Recall (1990), Dark Angel represents an important entry in the cycle of lower-budget sci-fi action films that flourished in this period. Its influence can be seen in later works like Timecop (1994) and Space Truckers (1996), which continued the tradition of mixing genre elements with high-concept sci-fi premises.
